messages.subject: Questions about generating asymmetrical components in bilat.symmetry
parts:
Dear geomorph team,

I am trying to understand bilat.symmetry  a bit more by running through the R script (https://github.com/geomorphR/geomorph/blob/Stable/R/bilat.symmetry.r) and encounter some questions related to calculating. I hope I understand the script right. I used the data(scallops) as the sample data, which has a sample size of 5, and run the code from the help file as well. I have some questions:

1. I found that the difference between two sides calculated for scallop.sym$asym.shapes are asymm.component <- avg.side.symm[indsq,] - avg.side.symm[-indsq,]) (line 329). This is equivalent to (reflection - original) using the scallop data as indisq = [2, 4, 6, 8, 10]
However, the calculation of differences between sides for directional (DA) and fluctuating asymmetry (FA) are all based on (original - reflection). For example, the FA component is:
  FA.component <- ind.mns[-indsq,] - ind.mns[indsq,] #for scallop, it is basically (original - reflection).
  FA.component <- simplify2array(lapply(1:n.ind, function(j)
  {t(matrix(FA.component[j,],k,p)) + mn.shape - mn.DA})) 
(lines 341-343)

It would not impact ANOVA. However, it makes checking the relationship between scallops.shape$symm.shape, $asymm. shape, $FA.component, and $DA.component a bit confusing. 
For example,  using the original bilat.symmtry(), I cannot get the asymmetrical shape of a specimen scallops.sym$asymm.shape[ , , 1] by using FA + DA + grand mean: 
scallops.sym$FA.component[, , 1] + (DA.component[, , 1]  - DA.component[, , 2]), 
#FA.componet = FA_residual + grand_mean
because FA is calculated from original - reflection, while asymmetry from reflection - original

I can obviously get the  $asymm.shape[ , , 1]  by  using the same way if I reverse the order of the reflection and original shapes so that asymmetric component beame (original - reflection): 
asymm.component <- avg.side.symm[-indsq,] - avg.side.symm[indsq,])  #In the original function, -indsq and indisq are reversed

Are there any specific reasons for calculating only the overall asymmetrical component as reflection - original, but FA and DA as original - reflections?

2. Why are the asymmetric components directly calculated from the difference between the original and reflection shapes, rather than divided by 2? If we just do (original - reflection), would it calculate left & right difference twice? 

Klingenberg 2015 pp. 865 also states that asymmetrical component should be original - symmetrical component, which is 1/2 of original - reflection, and DA = mean original - mean symmetrical = 1/2 * (mean original - mean reflection). 

3. Why did the DA.component only export the mean original and reflected shapes? In that case, would it be more straight forward to just export a single DA shape as mn.DA + grand_mean? I feel users can able to calculate left and right mean shape by simply do a mean(asymm.shape).

Thank you very much for your time!

Chi Zhang

Instructional Assistant Professor, 
Department of Biomedical Sciences,
Texas A&M University School of Dentistry, Dallas, TX
chi....@tamu.edu

parts:
Chi Zhang,

 

“Are there any specific reasons for calculating only the overall asymmetrical component as reflection - original, but FA and DA as original - reflections?”

 

  • No reason. It represents a vector of differences so one is just a sign-difference of the other.

 

“Why are the asymmetric components directly calculated from the difference between the original and reflection shapes, rather than divided by 2?”

 

  • It is a difference value not an average see the original papers on asymmetry analysis.

 

“Why did the DA.component only export the mean original and reflected shapes?”

 

  • Again this was the original definition of the directional asymmetry component this is also restated in the Klingenberg 2015 paper that you cited (pg. 865: Directional asymmetry is the average of the individual asymmetries …).

 

Dean

 

Dr. Dean C. Adams

Distinguished Professor of Evolutionary Biology

Department of Ecology, Evolution, and Organismal Biology

Iowa State University

  FA.component <- ind.mns[-indsq,] - ind.mns[indsq,] #for scallop, it is basically (original - reflection).
  FA.component <- simplify2array(lapply(1:n.ind, function(j)

Klingenberg 2015 pp. 865 also states that asymmetrical component should be original - symmetrical component, which is 1/2 of original - reflection, and DA = mean original - mean symmetrical = 1/2 * (mean original - mean reflection).

Thank you very much for your time!

parts:
Hi Dr. Adams,

Thank you very much for answering my questions. Yes, I agree that some problems are trivial and only about visualizations. And yes, I understand that the directional asymmetry is the mean asymmetry in a sample and the residuals of directional asymmetry can be got from using the scallop.symm$DA.component[, , 1] - scallop.symm$DA.component[, , 2].  

I'll go back to read Palmer's original papers about asymmetry to clarify these concepts again.

However, for Klingenberg 2015 I cited, other than the parts I quoted, there is also this "Directional asymmetry is the average of the individual asymmetries and can be computed from the difference of the average of all the original copies minus the overall symmetric consensus in the entire sample (or, equivalent but twice the magnitude, the average shape of all the original minus the average of all the reflected and relabeled copies). 

If I read it correctly, it shows that the DA component is (average original - average reflection)/2 = average asymmetry - average symmetry.

For example, for the codes extracted from the bilat.symmetry script using the scallop data https://github.com/chz31/OBIO_689_305_morphometrics/blob/main/test_bilat_asymm.R
In this script, I tried to use the (asymmetry + symmetry) to reconstruct the shape of the first specimen after a pooled GPA of reflections and original configurations.

After running this script, if I do:
specimen1_test <- (asymm.component[, , 1] - mn.shape) + symm.component[, , 1] #line 50
#The asymm.component is calculated from (reflection - original) + mn.shape based on the original bilat.symmetry script
#Thus, this is equivalent to (reflection -original) + symm.component of specimen1
I cannot recover the specimen 1's reflection of the original shape, which is A[, , 6] (because asymm.component is calculated from reflection - original).

However, if I do:
specimen1_test <- (asymm.component[, , 1] - mn.shape)/2 + symm.component[, , 1] #line 54
#I.e., the asymm residual is calculated as (reflection - original)/2
I can actually recover specimen 1's reflection A[, , 6]. Thus, should I consider (reflection - original)/2 (or (original - reflection)/2) as the actual asymmetrical component?

Using (original - reflection) without divided by 2 may still make sense since the 'sides' from ANOVA is just a comparison of average original and average reflection.

parts:
Again,

 

Asymmetry components by definition are  the difference between sides. Which comes first is completely arbitrary. R-L and L-R both describe the same FA vector, with the sign reversed. The same for object symmetry. Original – reflection or the opposite is arbitrary decision. There is no a biological nor mathematical  reason that one must precede the other ( the digitizing order of landmarks is completely arbitrary and reversing them would result in this order being reflected).

 

Klingenberg 2015 inserted an order because one must start somewhere. His downstream sentences follow from his decision of which he started with. That is all.

 

That being said,  it is inconvenient to have R-L for some components (asymm) and L-R for others (DA and FA). I will make that internally consistent in the next version of geomorph.

Dean

Sent: Wednesday, February 28, 2024 6:21 PM
To: geomorph R package <geomorph-...@googlegroups.com>
Subject: [geomorph-r-package] Questions about generating asymmetrical components in bilat.symmetry

 

Dear geomorph team,

 

I am trying to understand bilat.symmetry  a bit more by running through the R script (https://github.com/geomorphR/geomorph/blob/Stable/R/bilat.symmetry.r) and encounter some questions related to calculating. I hope I understand the script right. I used the data(scallops) as the sample data, which has a sample size of 5, and run the code from the help file as well. I have some questions:

 

1. I found that the difference between two sides calculated for scallop.sym$asym.shapes are asymm.component <- avg.side.symm[indsq,] - avg.side.symm[-indsq,]) (line 329). This is equivalent to (reflection - original) using the scallop data as indisq = [2, 4, 6, 8, 10]

However, the calculation of differences between sides for directional (DA) and fluctuating asymmetry (FA) are all based on (original - reflection). For example, the FA component is:

  FA.component <- ind.mns[-indsq,] - ind.mns[indsq,] #for scallop, it is basically (original - reflection).
  FA.component <- simplify2array(lapply(1:n.ind, function(j)

  {t(matrix(FA.component[j,],k,p)) + mn.shape - mn.DA})) 

(lines 341-343)

 

It would not impact ANOVA. However, it makes checking the relationship between scallops.shape$symm.shape, $asymm. shape, $FA.component, and $DA.component a bit confusing. 

For example,  using the original bilat.symmtry(), I cannot get the asymmetrical shape of a specimen scallops.sym$asymm.shape[ , , 1] by using FA + DA + grand mean: 

scallops.sym$FA.component[, , 1] + (DA.component[, , 1]  - DA.component[, , 2]), 

#FA.componet = FA_residual + grand_mean

because FA is calculated from original - reflection, while asymmetry from reflection - original

 

I can obviously get the  $asymm.shape[ , , 1]  by  using the same way if I reverse the order of the reflection and original shapes so that asymmetric component beame (original - reflection): 

asymm.component <- avg.side.symm[-indsq,] - avg.side.symm[indsq,])  #In the original function, -indsq and indisq are reversed

 

Are there any specific reasons for calculating only the overall asymmetrical component as reflection - original, but FA and DA as original - reflections?

 

2. Why are the asymmetric components directly calculated from the difference between the original and reflection shapes, rather than divided by 2? If we just do (original - reflection), would it calculate left & right difference twice? 

 

Klingenberg 2015 pp. 865 also states that asymmetrical component should be original - symmetrical component, which is 1/2 of original - reflection, and DA = mean original - mean symmetrical = 1/2 * (mean original - mean reflection). 

 

3. Why did the DA.component only export the mean original and reflected shapes? In that case, would it be more straight forward to just export a single DA shape as mn.DA + grand_mean? I feel users can able to calculate left and right mean shape by simply do a mean(asymm.shape).

Thank you very much for your time!

 

Chi Zhang

Instructional Assistant Professor, 

Department of Biomedical Sciences,

Texas A&M University School of Dentistry, Dallas, TX

chi....@tamu.edu

parts:
Hi Dr. Adams,

Thanks again for the clarification of the concepts! Yes, it would be nice to make the representation of different asymmetrical components internally consistent.

Best,
Chi
On Sun, Mar 3, 2024 at 9:25 AM Adams, Dean [EEOB] <dca...@iastate.edu> wrote:

Again,

 

Asymmetry components by definition are  the difference between sides. Which comes first is completely arbitrary. R-L and L-R both describe the same FA vector, with the sign reversed. The same for object symmetry. Original – reflection or the opposite is arbitrary decision. There is no a biological nor mathematical  reason that one must precede the other ( the digitizing order of landmarks is completely arbitrary and reversing them would result in this order being reflected).

 

Klingenberg 2015 inserted an order because one must start somewhere. His downstream sentences follow from his decision of which he started with. That is all.

 

That being said,  it is inconvenient to have R-L for some components (asymm) and L-R for others (DA and FA). I will make that internally consistent in the next version of geomorph.

 

Dean

 

Dr. Dean C. Adams

Distinguished Professor of Evolutionary Biology

Department of Ecology, Evolution, and Organismal Biology

Iowa State University

https://faculty.sites.iastate.edu/dcadams/

From: geomorph-...@googlegroups.com <geomorph-...@googlegroups.com> On Behalf Of Chi Zhang
Sent: Saturday, March 2, 2024 10:08 PM
To: geomorph-...@googlegroups.com
Subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Questions about generating asymmetrical components in bilat.symmetry

 

Hi Dr. Adams,

 

Thank you very much for answering my questions. Yes, I agree that some problems are trivial and only about visualizations. And yes, I understand that the directional asymmetry is the mean asymmetry in a sample and the residuals of directional asymmetry can be got from using the scallop.symm$DA.component[, , 1] - scallop.symm$DA.component[, , 2].  

 

I'll go back to read Palmer's original papers about asymmetry to clarify these concepts again.

 

However, for Klingenberg 2015 I cited, other than the parts I quoted, there is also this "Directional asymmetry is the average of the individual asymmetries and can be computed from the difference of the average of all the original copies minus the overall symmetric consensus in the entire sample (or, equivalent but twice the magnitude, the average shape of all the original minus the average of all the reflected and relabeled copies). 

 

If I read it correctly, it shows that the DA component is (average original - average reflection)/2 = average asymmetry - average symmetry.

 

For example, for the codes extracted from the bilat.symmetry script using the scallop data https://github.com/chz31/OBIO_689_305_morphometrics/blob/main/test_bilat_asymm.R

In this script, I tried to use the (asymmetry + symmetry) to reconstruct the shape of the first specimen after a pooled GPA of reflections and original configurations.

 

After running this script, if I do:

specimen1_test <- (asymm.component[, , 1] - mn.shape) + symm.component[, , 1] #line 50

#The asymm.component is calculated from (reflection - original) + mn.shape based on the original bilat.symmetry script

#Thus, this is equivalent to (reflection -original) + symm.component of specimen1

I cannot recover the specimen 1's reflection of the original shape, which is A[, , 6] (because asymm.component is calculated from reflection - original).

 

However, if I do:

specimen1_test <- (asymm.component[, , 1] - mn.shape)/2 + symm.component[, , 1] #line 54

#I.e., the asymm residual is calculated as (reflection - original)/2

I can actually recover specimen 1's reflection A[, , 6]. Thus, should I consider (reflection - original)/2 (or (original - reflection)/2) as the actual asymmetrical component?

 

Using (original - reflection) without divided by 2 may still make sense since the 'sides' from ANOVA is just a comparison of average original and average reflection.

 

 

 

 

 

On Sat, Mar 2, 2024 at 9:07 AM Adams, Dean [EEOB] <dca...@iastate.edu> wrote:

One other thing I forgot to mention. Directional asymmetry is generally considered to be a population level parameter. For this reason it is found from the mean (see Palmer’s work in the 1980s for a more thorough description).

 

Dean

Iowa State University

From: geomorph-...@googlegroups.com <geomorph-...@googlegroups.com> On Behalf Of Adams, Dean [EEOB]
Sent: Friday, March 1, 2024 5:14 PM
To: geomorph-...@googlegroups.com
Subject: RE: [geomorph-r-package] Questions about generating asymmetrical components in bilat.symmetry

 

Chi Zhang,

 

“Are there any specific reasons for calculating only the overall asymmetrical component as reflection - original, but FA and DA as original - reflections?”

 

  • No reason. It represents a vector of differences so one is just a sign-difference of the other.

 

“Why are the asymmetric components directly calculated from the difference between the original and reflection shapes, rather than divided by 2?”

 

  • It is a difference value not an average see the original papers on asymmetry analysis.

 

“Why did the DA.component only export the mean original and reflected shapes?”

 

  • Again this was the original definition of the directional asymmetry component this is also restated in the Klingenberg 2015 paper that you cited (pg. 865: Directional asymmetry is the average of the individual asymmetries …).

 

Dean
